record.title: A semi-implicit unified gas-kinetic wave-particle method with energy-conserving electromagnetic coupling for multiscale plasmas
record.abstract: Abstract: In multiscale plasmas, kinetic regions coexist with collision-dominated, strongly magnetized and quasi-neutral ones. In these regions, the collision time, the cyclotron period and the plasma period, respectively, are far shorter than the flow time scales. Schemes that treat the collisions and the field coupling explicitly must take time steps below these times and below the light-crossing time of a cell. This paper presents a semi-implicit unified gas-kinetic wave-particle (UGKWP) method for the multispecies Vlasov-Maxwell system with Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook collisions. The electric field follows from a reformulated Maxwell equation, a single linear system with a unique solution for any time step. Its current response is built from the implicit-midpoint velocity map, which then pushes the particles and the hydrodynamic wave alike. The field step conserves the discrete total energy exactly and remains stable without resolving the cyclotron period, the plasma period or the light-crossing time, so that the time step follows from the flow and sound speeds. A Gauss's law correction adjusts the electric field and the joint charge of particles and wave while conserving the mass, momentum and energy of every charged species. The method reproduces whistler waves and electron plasma waves from Landau damping to collision-dominated oscillations. It agrees with particle-in-cell, two-fluid and magnetohydrodynamic references in a Brio-Wu problem from weak to strong collisionality and magnetization, the Orszag-Tang vortex and collisionless magnetic reconnection. It needs far less CPU time than either the UGKWP method with an explicit solver for the perfectly hyperbolic Maxwell equations or a deterministic multiscale kinetic scheme. In collisional plasmas, it also needs less CPU time than an implicit particle-in-cell method with the same collision operator, increasingly so as collisions strengthen.

title: Unified gas-kinetic wave-particle method for multiscale phonon transport
An implicit unified gas-kinetic wave–particle method for radiative transport process
crossref.abstract: <jats:p>The unified gas-kinetic wave–particle method (UGKWP) has been developed for the multiscale gas, plasma, and multiphase flow transport processes for the past years. In this work, we propose an implicit UGKWP (IUGKWP) method to remove the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy time step constraint. Based on the local integral solution of the radiative transfer equation (RTE), the particle transport processes are categorized into the long-λ streaming process and the short-λ streaming process compared to a local physical characteristic time tp. In the construction of the IUGKWP method, the long-λ streaming process is tracked by the implicit Monte Carlo method; the short-λ streaming process is evolved by solving the implicit moment equations; and the photon distribution is closed by a local integral solution of RTE. In the IUGKWP method, the multiscale flux of radiation energy and the multiscale closure of photon distribution are constructed based on the local integral solution. The IUGKWP method preserves the second-order asymptotic expansion of RTE in the optically thick regime and adapts its computational complexity to the flow regime. The numerical dissipation is well controlled, and the teleportation error is significantly reduced in the optically thick regime. The computational complexity of the IUGKWP method decreases exponentially as the Knudsen number approaches zero, and the computational efficiency is remarkably improved in the optically thick regime. The IUGKWP is formulated on a generalized unstructured mesh, and multidimensional 2D and 3D algorithms are developed. Numerical tests are presented to validate the capability of IUGKWP in capturing the multiscale photon transport process. The algorithm and code will apply in the engineering applications of inertial confinement fusion.</jats:p>

title: Unified gas-kinetic wave-particle method for multiscale flow modeling and computation

record.title: Bayesian optimization of longitudinally aligned CNT targets for 800 nm laser wakefield acceleration in the bubble regime
record.abstract: Abstract: Laser wakefield acceleration (LWFA) in solid-density plasmas can reach accelerating gradients in the TeV/m range, well above those of gaseous media, provided the driver is matched to the plasma. In nanostructured solids, this matching can be achieved by controlling the spacing between the nanostructures to reduce the effective density, enabling infrared pulses to excite wakefields in the bubble regime. Following numerical demonstrations with carbon nanotube (CNT) bundles on concentric cylindrical shells, a simpler, experimentally more accessible longitudinally aligned CNT (LA-CNT) target is investigated here, with the bundles on a triangular lattice within a square cross section and an optional central aperture. Three-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations are coupled with Bayesian optimization to vary the effective density, target length, bundle radius and aperture radius for a fixed 100 mJ, few-cycle, 800 nm laser pulse, maximizing the laser-to-beam energy conversion efficiency for electrons above 20 MeV. With the aperture radius constrained to at least 0.5 $\mu$m, the best target operates in the bubble regime and reaches an efficiency of 24.6%, delivering a 673 pC bunch with a mean energy of 36.6 MeV and a quasi-monoenergetic peak near 46 MeV, against 19% for the concentric-shell target under identical conditions. When the aperture is allowed to vanish, the optimization converges to denser and shorter targets, the efficiency peaks at 25.8%, and the best configurations deliver a higher charge at the cost of a lower peak energy and about 50% larger divergence; aperture-free targets among them retain a mean efficiency of 24.1%. The optimized targets are robust to random bundle displacements that preserve the effective density. By eliminating the need to pattern a micrometre-scale opening, aperture-free targets may facilitate proof-of-principle experiments on solid-state LWFA.

title: Numerical study of electron acceleration in structured CNT targets via self-injection in a wakefield bubble driven by an 800 nm laser
crossref.abstract: Laser wakefield acceleration (LWFA) may achieve TeV/m gradients using high-density solid-state plasmas as accelerating media. However, the application of bulk solid materials requires attosecond laser pulses, such as X-ray lasers, to drive wakefields at these high densities. Additionally, the short wakefield wavelengths associated with solid-state plasmas greatly limit the accelerating length. An alternative approach employs 2D carbon-based nanomaterials, like graphene or carbon nanotubes (CNTs), configured into structured targets. These nanostructures are designed with voids or low-density regions to effectively reduce the overall plasma density. This reduction enables the use of longer-wavelength lasers and also extends the plasma wavelength and the acceleration length. In this study, we present, to our knowledge, the first numerical demonstration of electron acceleration via self-injection into a wakefield bubble driven by an infrared laser pulse in structured CNT targets, similar to the behavior observed in gaseous plasmas for LWFA in the nonlinear (or bubble) regime. Using the PIConGPU code, bundles of CNTs are modeled in a 3D geometry as 25 nm-thick carbon tubes with an initial density of 1022 cm−3. The carbon plasma is ionized by a three-cycle, 800 nm wavelength laser pulse with a peak intensity of 1021W cm−2, achieving an effective plasma density of 1020 cm−3. The same laser also drives the wakefield bubble, responsible for the electron self-injection and acceleration. Simulation results indicate that fs-long electron bunches with hundreds of pC charge can be self-injected and accelerated at gradients exceeding 1 TeV/m. Both charge and accelerating gradient figures are unprecedented when compared with LWFA in gaseous plasma.

title: Direct laser acceleration in the bubble regime of laser wakefield acceleration
Dephasingless laser wakefield acceleration in the bubble regime
crossref.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Laser wakefield accelerators (LWFAs) have electric fields that are orders of magnitude larger than those of conventional accelerators, promising an attractive, small-scale alternative for next-generation light sources and lepton colliders. The maximum energy gain in a single-stage LWFA is limited by dephasing, which occurs when the trapped particles outrun the accelerating phase of the wakefield. Here, we demonstrate that a single space–time structured laser pulse can be used for ionization injection and electron acceleration over many dephasing lengths in the bubble regime. Simulations of a dephasingless laser wakefield accelerator driven by a 6.2-J laser pulse show 25 pC of injected charge accelerated over 20 dephasing lengths (1.3 cm) to a maximum energy of 2.1 GeV. The space–time structured laser pulse features an ultrashort, programmable-trajectory focus. Accelerating the focus, reducing the focused spot-size variation, and mitigating unwanted self-focusing stabilize the electron acceleration, which improves beam quality and leads to projected energy gains of 125 GeV in a single, sub-meter stage driven by a 500-J pulse.</jats:p>

record.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>CR-39 offers numerous advantages for neutron detection, yet its strong angular dependence has long compromised the accuracy of measurements. To address this issue, this work proposes a novel cubic neutron detector consisting of six CR-39 elements. By taking the average response of the six elements as the measurement metric, the angular dependence is effectively suppressed. To accommodate the broad energy range of realistic neutron fields, a compact dual-converter structure is designed, in which polyethylene and boron nitride converters are coupled to the two faces of CR-39 element for fast- and thermal-neutron detection, respectively. Simulation results show that the angular variation in detector response remains below 12% for both fast- and thermal-neutron detection over the full solid angle, whereas a conventional single CR-39 element exhibits a response variation exceeding 300%. This superior angular independence has also been verified experimentally.</jats:p>
title: A novel angle-independent neutron detector based on CR-39

record.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Neutron spectrum unfolding based on neutron activation reactions is an inherently ill-posed inverse problem that is difficult to validate experimentally. This study extends the performance evaluation of the SpecKit software previously published in SoftwareX, with a focus on quantifying the effect of energy-group structure on unfolding accuracy. The ground-truth neutron spectrum was generated using MCNP simulations. The prior spectrum was modeled under the same geometric configuration; however, compared with the ground-truth spectrum, the cement layer in the 60-, 113- and 240-group cases was uniformly reduced by 3 cm to simulate scattering interference and geometric simplification commonly encountered in real-world applications. Comparative unfolding with SpecKit using 60-, 113- and 240-group structures shows that the mean activity error (ERRE) of calculated activities is significantly reduced from 0.165 to 0.050, while the integrated flux also approaches the ground-truth value more closely (ground-truth: 1.606 × 10
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                     n/cm
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    /s; 60-group: 1.065 × 10
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    ; 240-group: 1.578 × 10
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    ). These empirical results demonstrate that, within the SpecKit framework, adopting a finer energy-group structure effectively mitigates the ill-posed nature of the problem, enhances numerical stability and reconstruction fidelity, and provides a reliable, reproducible software platform for nuclear engineering education and practical neutron field analysis. The open-source SpecKit toolkit is freely available at GitHub.
                  </jats:p>
title: Effects of energy-group resolution on SpecKit-based neutron spectrum unfolding

record.abstract: <jats:p>We present a data-driven plasma fluid closure for both linear and nonlinear electrostatic Landau damping in one dimension. A Fourier neural operator (FNO) is trained online within a differentiable fluid solver, with the loss computed on trajectories produced by the closed fluid simulation rather than on individual kinetic snapshots. The closure is non-Markovian, acting on a trailing window of the resolved-moment history so as to represent the memory of the unresolved dynamics. We demonstrate that a single FNO trained in this way reproduces both linear and nonlinear Landau damping, generalises to unseen initial perturbation amplitudes lying between those used in training, and remains numerically stable when deployed in independent fluid simulations. In the nonlinear regime the learned heat flux reproduces the resolved-moment dynamics without matching the kinetic heat flux pointwise, behaving as an effective closure that carries the influence of the unresolved dynamics through the resolved-field history, though the learned specific flux is expected to depend on the numerical scheme and training data. A sensitivity analysis of the trained model shows that it computes a genuine moment-to-flux relation whose reliance on the memory window is structured rather than uniform, concentrating at lags spaced by the oscillation period.</jats:p>
title: A neural operator closure for Landau damping in electrostatic plasma
